text.en: Early astronauts looked back at the Earth and called it the blue planet. Almost three-fourths of its surface is covered with water, and the rest is land. In this chapter we meet the five oceans, the seven continents and the islands in between. We also see how oceans give us rain and oxygen, and how they can bring storms and tsunamis.

Rotate a globe slowly, or look at a picture of the Earth taken from the Moon. The most widespread colour is blue, and blue stands for water. Almost three-fourths of the surface is water, which is why the Earth is called the blue planet. The largest water bodies are called oceans. Their smaller extensions have names such as sea, bay and gulf. The brown colour in the picture is land, a little over one-fourth of the globe. A large body of land is a landmass, and a large continuous expanse of land is a continent. Oceans and continents are not spread equally between the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. Both of them shape the climate and affect plants, animals and people. The Indian Navy badge carries the motto Sam noh Varunah, meaning, Be auspicious to us, O Varuna. Varuna is a Vedic deity linked with the oceans, the sky and water. Seawater is salty and unfit for most land animals, including humans. Fresh water is a very small part of all the water on the planet. It is found in glaciers, rivers, lakes, the atmosphere and underground, where it is called groundwater. That is why people speak of a water crisis even though the planet has so much water.
The world map shows five oceans: the Pacific, the Atlantic, the Indian, the Arctic and the Southern or Antarctic Ocean. The lines that divide them are only conventions. In nature the oceans are joined, and seawater keeps flowing from one to another carrying marine life. Marine flora includes tiny plants called algae and many kinds of seaweed. Marine fauna includes thousands of kinds of fish, dolphins, whales and many deep-sea creatures. By size, the Pacific is the largest, then the Atlantic, then the Indian Ocean third and the Southern Ocean fourth. The Arctic is the smallest. The Indian Ocean has Asia to the north, Africa to the west and Australia to the east, with the Southern Ocean to the south. On either side of India lie two parts of it: the Arabian Sea in the west and the Bay of Bengal in the east.
White shapes in the picture of the Earth are clouds. They bring rain to the continents. The monsoon rains that India expects each summer begin over the ocean, and without them our farming and all life would suffer. Oceans also give rise to violent storms with extreme rain or strong winds, such as cyclones, which can badly damage coasts. A tsunami is a huge, powerful wave, usually caused by a strong earthquake or a volcanic eruption on the ocean floor. It can travel thousands of kilometres and flood coastal areas. On 26 December 2004 an earthquake near Indonesia caused a tsunami that struck India and 13 other countries around the Indian Ocean. More than two lakh people died. The Andaman and Nicobar Islands and the coasts of Tamil Nadu and Kerala were badly hit. Tsunamis are rare, but they can often be detected before they reach a coast. Many countries, including India, take part in the Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System, and India has a National Disaster Management Authority to handle disasters.
How many continents are there? The answer depends on how we count. We can count anywhere from four to seven. North America and South America are usually two continents, but they can be seen as one landmass. Europe and Asia are usually two, although the map shows one landmass, which geologists often call Eurasia. Africa and Eurasia are usually two but are sometimes counted as one. Counting four gives Africa-Eurasia, America, Antarctica and Australia. Five gives Africa, America, Antarctica, Australia and Eurasia. Six splits America into North and South America. Seven, the most widely used, gives Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America. The five Olympic rings stand for the five inhabited continents: Africa, America, Asia, Australia and Europe.
The continents do not include all the land. Smaller pieces of land surrounded by water on all sides are called islands. Continents are also surrounded by water, but they are too large to be called islands. There are lakhs of islands of very different sizes. Greenland is the largest island in the world. India has more than 1300 small islands. There are two major groups: the Andaman and Nicobar Islands in the Bay of Bengal and the Lakshadweep Islands in the Arabian Sea. Since 1981 the Indian Antarctica Programme has explored Antarctica, a continent with a very cold climate. India set up its first scientific base there in 1983, called Dakshin Gangotri, and later two more bases. About 40 teams of Indian scientists have studied climate and environment there.
Oceans send rain to the continents as part of the Earth water cycle. Without oceans there would be no rainfall and the Earth would be a desert. More than half of the world oxygen is produced by the plants of the oceans, which is why oceans are called the lungs of the planet. They help regulate the climate and sustain life. From early times people used oceans and seas to migrate, to trade, to carry out military campaigns and for food from fishing. Coastal peoples everywhere have tales of sea gods, sea monsters and treasures from the sea. The United Nations has marked 8 June as World Oceans Day. Human activity pollutes the oceans. Several million tonnes of plastic waste reach them every year and choke marine life. Overfishing, which means catching too much fish, also reduces marine life. Protecting the oceans is our collective responsibility for the future of the planet and of humanity.

board.text: Oceans and life, and how we can protect them

problem.en: The oceans in size order: from the biggest to the smallest

text.en: Start with the largest, which is the Pacific.

why.en: The Pacific is the largest ocean in the world.

text.en: Next comes the Atlantic.

why.en: The Atlantic is second in size.

text.en: Then the Indian Ocean third and the Southern Ocean fourth.
The smallest is the Arctic Ocean.

why.en: The Arctic is the fifth and smallest.

prompt.en: Explain how oceans help us and how they can also harm us.

requiredIdeas.en: Oceans cover almost three-fourths of the Earth surface and send rain through the water cycle
Their plants give more than half of the world oxygen
Oceans give food, trade routes and cultures but can bring cyclones and tsunamis
People pollute oceans with plastic and overfish, so we must protect them

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking oceans are separate and do not mix
Thinking seawater can be drunk like fresh water
Thinking there are exactly seven continents in every count

points.en: Almost three-fourths of the Earth is water and a little over one-fourth is land.
The five oceans are the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic, and they are all joined.
Continents can be counted as four, five, six or seven; seven is most used.
Islands are small landmasses surrounded by water. India has more than 1300, in the Andaman and Nicobar and the Lakshadweep groups.
Oceans give rain, oxygen, food, trade routes and culture, but also cyclones and tsunamis, and pollution and overfishing threaten them.
